v.why: Filling an empty input-output edge with a residual shortcut gives large gains (exps 22, 26, 28), unlike overwriting an existing op.
Replacing the 0->3 conv with a skip often removes the cell's main or only conv, which hurts badly (exps 24, 25, 27).
When edge 0 is absent, edge 3 is often the only route from input to output, so deleting it collapses the network (exp 2).
Deleting edge 0 hurts more when it removes a 3x3 conv than when it removes a skip or pool (exps 84, 87, 90 vs 82, 86).
Pruning a parameter-free skip on edge 1 is harmless or even helpful, whereas pruning a conv there loses capacity (exps 54, 56 vs 51, 59).
Removing a skip on edge 5 costs little or helps in skip-heavy cells, while removing a conv on edge 5 hurts (exps 75, 77 vs 71, 72).
Swapping a 3x3 conv for a pool on edge 4 loses capacity, while swapping out a skip or an empty edge is near-neutral (exps 46, 47, 50 vs 42, 43).
Skip-dominated cells lack convolutions, so adding a 3x3 conv on edge 5 yields huge gains (exps 16, 18).
When edge 1 is a skip the cell tends to be conv-poor, so adding a conv on edge 0 helps much more (exps 35, 36, 40 vs 31-34).
Pool-dominated cells gain greatly from any learnable conv on the output edge (exps 95, 96 vs 91, 99, 100).

raw:
I grounded each hypothesis in the 100 experiments and in known NAS-Bench-201 structure. Two patterns drive most of them:

- **Conv-starved cells benefit most from adding a conv.** Cells built entirely from skip or avg-pool edges gain +30 to +50 points on CIFAR when a conv is added.
- **Removing an edge hurts most when it breaks the only path or removes the only conv.** Rewiring the 0→3 shortcut follows the same logic: adding a skip there helps when it fills an empty edge, and hurts when it replaces a conv.
